**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Paper 2: Section A - Composition; Section B - Prescribed Texts; Section C - Creative Writing. Duration: two hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised answer will earn you little or no marks.

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **d)** Acquiring education in your country is very difficult for the average citizen. Suggest measures that could make it easier for them.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the value of education and the obstacles faced by ordinary families.
2. The difficulties (cost, distance, overcrowding, gender, insecurity, unemployment).
3. Measures by government: free education, scholarships, schools and teachers in rural areas.
4. Measures by technology, vocational training, communities and parents.
5. Conclusion: cooperation removes the barriers.

**Model essay (513 words)**

Education is the key that opens the door to a better life, yet in many countries the average citizen must struggle even to reach that door. In our country, a child from an ordinary family often meets obstacles at every stage, from the first day of nursery school to the last day at university. Unless these obstacles are removed, the dream of national development will remain only a dream.

The difficulties are many. The first is cost: although primary education is officially free, parents still pay for uniforms, books, parent-teacher association levies and examination fees, which weigh heavily on a family that lives on a small farm or on petty trading. Secondly, schools are unevenly distributed; in remote villages, children walk several kilometres each morning to a building with a leaking roof, no desks and one teacher for several classes. Thirdly, in towns, overcrowded classrooms in which a hundred pupils share a single teacher make real learning almost impossible. Moreover, girls are often kept at home to work or married early, and children in areas affected by insecurity have seen their schools closed. As a result, thousands of children drop out before they can read and write properly. Finally, graduates who cannot find jobs discourage parents from investing in education at all.

What can be done? First, the government must make basic education genuinely free by paying the fees, supplying textbooks and punishing the illegal charges demanded by some schools. Scholarships and school-feeding programmes should be offered to gifted pupils from poor families and to girls, so that talent is no longer the privilege of wealth. Examination fees, which now exclude many bright pupils, should be reduced or paid for the neediest candidates. More schools must be built and equipped in rural areas, and teachers must be recruited in sufficient numbers and given good salaries and housing allowances, so that they accept posts in villages.

Technology can also help. Radio and television lessons, low-cost tablets and community libraries with internet access allow pupils far from the cities to reach the same knowledge as their urban peers. Teachers should also receive regular training in modern methods, so that even a poorly equipped classroom can offer quality teaching. In addition, vocational and technical training should be expanded so that those who prefer practical skills can learn a trade and find work, which would restore the confidence of parents in schooling.

Other actors must play their part. Communities can form school-support associations to build classrooms and mend roofs; churches, companies and wealthy citizens can sponsor pupils; and non-governmental organisations can run evening classes for dropouts and adults. Parents, for their part, must give education priority over expensive ceremonies and make sure that their daughters sit beside their sons in the classroom.

In conclusion, education is difficult to acquire not because our young people lack ability, but because the path to it is blocked by cost, distance and neglect. If the state, the community and the family work together, those barriers can be removed, and the average citizen will find that learning is as easy as dreaming.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | Both parts: a brief account of the difficulties and, above all, concrete and realistic measures, each with a reason; paragraphs in logical order, 500 to 550 words. |
| Expression | 8 | Formal, persuasive register; modal verbs of suggestion (should, must, could), varied connectors, precise vocabulary. |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation. |

**Common errors**

- Spending the whole essay on the difficulties and giving only one or two vague measures: the question asks you to SUGGEST measures.
- Suggestions that are unrealistic or unexplained (for example 'build schools everywhere') without saying who should act and how.
